---
title: "Interactive Robot Navigation through the Integration of Human Inputs and Environmental Information"
bibliography: references.bib
link-citations: true
---

Autonomous navigation is a fundamental capability for mobile robots. In conventional navigation systems, robots perceive their surroundings through sensors, construct a structural representation of the environment, and select actions of path that satisfy geometric and kinematic constraints. Humans appearing in the environment are often represented in the same format as the environment, for example as elements in object sets or as inaccessible grids in occupation maps. This representation has supported substantial progress in human-aware and socially aware navigation, where robots are expected not only to avoid collisions but also to respect human comfort, social conventions, and motion patterns [@kruse2013; @moller2021]. As robots move into everyday human environments, navigation increasingly involves direct interaction with people rather than merely motion around them. Effective interactive navigation therefore requires a unified framework that integrates human inputs and environmental information while preserving the essential information and constraints of both. This integration is particularly challenging for online physical interaction, natural-language instructions, and data-driven navigation frameworks.

Human input during navigation can occur at different levels and through different modalities. At a relatively low level, a person may physically push, pull, or guide a robot, and interaction forces can be converted into motion commands while obstacle avoidance maintains safety [@fremy2014]. At a higher level, a person may communicate a navigation goal or route using natural language. Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), for example, requires an embodied agent to interpret natural-language instructions in relation to visual observations and execute corresponding navigation actions [@anderson2018]. Recent work has expanded VLN towards spatial reasoning and foundation models, further connecting linguistic instructions with environmental representations and embodied decision-making [@zhang2024]. These developments show that interactive robot navigation is moving beyond purely geometric sensing towards heterogeneous human inputs containing intention, preference, semantic meaning, and task-level constraints.

Despite this progress, human input and environmental information are still commonly handled through task-specific representations and mechanisms. Conventional navigation can conveniently represent both static obstacles and moving people geometrically because their influence on navigation can be expressed through occupancy, distance, velocity, or collision constraints. However, this common representation becomes increasingly difficult to maintain when interaction involves higher-level or multimodal information. A force applied by a human represents not only a physical quantity but potentially an immediate motion intention. A physical connection, such as guiding or pulling through a handle or cable, introduces continuous interaction constraints between the human and robot. A language instruction can encode goals, landmarks, spatial relations, route preferences, and sequential actions that cannot be adequately represented as occupied cells or object trajectories. Thus, handling human interaction simply as another component of the sensed environment risks losing information that is essential for understanding the human’s intention and behaviour.

Existing research addresses important parts of this problem but often from different perspectives. Human-aware and social navigation mostly focus on safe, comfortable, and socially appropriate motion around people [@kruse2013; @singamaneni2024]. Physical human–robot interaction studies how forces or direct contact can be incorporated into robot control [@fremy2014]. In parallel, VLN focuses on grounding linguistic instructions in visual and spatial observations [@anderson2018; @zhang2024]. Together, these directions reveal a broader architectural challenge: human inputs may be physical, semantic, continuous, discrete, low-level, or high-level, whereas environmental information is commonly represented through geometric and semantic models designed primarily for autonomous perception and planning. As the diversity of human input increases, developing separate navigation mechanisms for each modality may make the overall system difficult to generalise and coordinate.

This shortage matters because successful task completion alone is insufficient for interactive navigation. A robot may reach its destination while responding poorly to the person interacting with it. Conversely, a robot may react smoothly to human input but fail to complete the navigation task safely or efficiently. Evaluation of social robot navigation therefore needs to consider both navigation performance and human-centred interaction quality rather than only geometric success [@francis2025]. The central research gap is the lack of a navigation framework that can systematically integrate heterogeneous human inputs with environmental information while preserving both task performance and interaction performance. Addressing this gap could allow richer human inputs without forcing every interaction into the same low-level environmental representation.

Therefore, this research aims to develop interactive robot navigation methods that integrate human inputs with environmental information for unified navigation decision-making. The first objective is to investigate how physical human inputs can be incorporated with environmental constraints to achieve safe and effective interaction during navigation. The second objective is to investigate how high-level language instructions can be connected with spatial and semantic environmental structures so that a robot can infer navigation decisions from both linguistic intent and perceived surroundings. Building on these studies, the broader objective is to establish a framework that can accommodate increasingly high-level, multimodal, and heterogeneous human inputs while maintaining robust navigation performance.

Accordingly, this research asks how complex human inputs and environmental information can be represented and integrated for interactive robot navigation, and how such integration affects both task success and interaction quality. Ultimately, the research seeks to enable robots to maintain a high task success rate while also achieving strong interaction performance in terms of safety, comfort, efficiency, and stability, even when human input becomes more complex and multimodal. Such a capability would support the transition from robots that merely navigate around people to robots that can navigate with people and according to their intentions.
